paragraphs: Recognizing a whole object is only part of understanding it in three dimensions. A system may also need to distinguish its parts and the materials associated with them. This paper introduces 3DCoMPaT200 to broaden the range of objects, parts, and materials available for studying that compositional understanding.

The dataset contains 200 object categories, 1,031 fine-grained part categories, and 293 material classes that can be applied to object parts. Compared with the earlier 3DCoMPaT dataset, it provides approximately five times the object vocabulary and almost four times the number of part categories. This expansion supports more varied combinations of object structure and material appearance.

The authors also introduce Compositional Part Shape Retrieval, using ULIP to retrieve shapes from text descriptions of one, three, or six parts. They report improved retrieval performance as the number of style compositions increases. These results support the value of compositional data for learning relationships between language and complex 3D shapes, alongside the dataset's contribution of substantially broader category coverage.
neurips-2024-3dcompat200-language-ground.tldr: 3DCoMPaT200 expands part-and-material understanding to 200 object categories and introduces shape retrieval from textual part descriptions.

paragraphs: Large multimodal models connect encoders for individual kinds of input with a language model, but the meaning of their internal representations can be difficult to interpret. This paper investigates whether those representations can be understood through concepts that have recognizable meanings in both images and text.

The proposed framework applies dictionary learning to token representations. It learns a collection of elements that serve as the framework's concepts, providing a way to describe representations through these learned components. The authors find that the resulting concepts have meaningful visual and textual grounding, which is why they call them multimodal concepts.

The evaluation examines the concepts both qualitatively and quantitatively, including how well they correspond to visual and textual content and how distinct different concepts are from one another. The authors also show that the concepts help interpret representations of test examples. The contribution is a concrete framework for examining what a multimodal model represents internally, with evaluation focused on whether its explanatory components are meaningful across both modalities.
neurips-2024-a-concept-based-explainabil.tldr: Dictionary learning extracts concepts grounded in both images and text to help interpret large multimodal models' internal representations.

paragraphs: Drawing in the air could make hand motion a convenient way to communicate visually, but existing tools often require specialized hardware or markers. Producing an attractive drawing also demands skill. AirSketch explores a more accessible approach: generating a coherent sketch directly from hand motion while retaining the essential visual information in the movement.

The method trains a controllable image diffusion model to translate noisy images of tracked hand motion into clean sketches. Its training procedure uses augmentations in a self-supervised setup. This gives the model a way to learn the transformation from degraded motion traces to refined drawings, with the tracking input providing control over the result.

The authors introduce two air-drawing datasets and report that controllable diffusion can produce clear sketches even from highly noisy inputs. The finding extends its demonstrated usefulness beyond photorealistic generation guided by precise spatial information. The paper presents this as an initial step toward drawing without markers, with potential relevance to augmented and virtual reality.
neurips-2024-airsketch-generative-motion.tldr: AirSketch uses controllable diffusion to turn noisy hand-motion traces into clear sketches while preserving their essential visual cues.

paragraphs: Predicting an unwanted outcome does not by itself explain what action could prevent it. The avoiding undesired future problem addresses that decision. An existing approach, rehearsal learning, uses influence relationships among variables to guide prevention, but changing relationships can undermine its effectiveness when the environment is no longer stationary.

This paper introduces a sequential method that updates estimates of those changing influence relationships. It also includes the cost of taking action in the decision problem. Together, these changes aim to keep prevention decisions responsive to the current environment while seeking actions that avoid unwanted outcomes at minimal cost.

For linear Gaussian cases, the authors prove that their formulation can be converted into a convex quadratically constrained quadratic program, a tractable class of optimization problems. This establishes a polynomial-time rehearsal-based approach in that setting. Theoretical and experimental results support its effectiveness and efficiency under certain circumstances. The significance is the combination of adaptation and action cost, with the computational result tied specifically to the stated linear Gaussian setting.
neurips-2024-avoiding-undesired-future-w.tldr: The method updates changing influence relationships to prevent unwanted outcomes at low action cost, with polynomial-time optimization in linear Gaussian cases.

paragraphs: Adversarial examples alter an image so that a classifier makes an incorrect judgment. This paper approaches their construction through the meaning people perceive in an image. It proposes representing subjective understanding of image semantics as a probability distribution, allowing that understanding to participate directly in the generation process.

The resulting method can make substantial changes at the pixel level while preserving the image's overall semantics. The authors report that these changes remain difficult for human observers to detect. The central idea is that the extent of pixel modification and the preservation of perceived meaning can behave differently, creating room for changes that challenge a classifier without obviously changing the image for a person.

In the reported experiments, the proposed methods achieve higher success rates against adversarial defenses while remaining difficult for humans to notice. The authors attribute improved deception of defended classifiers to the more extensive pixel modifications their approach permits. The contribution is a probabilistic way to incorporate semantic judgments into adversarial generation, supported by these empirical findings.
neurips-2024-constructing-semantics-awar.tldr: A probabilistic representation of image semantics enables adversarial changes that preserve perceived meaning while achieving higher attack success in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Static language-model benchmarks face two problems: their examples may become contaminated by training data, and their difficulty does not adapt as models improve. DARG addresses these concerns by extending existing benchmarks with newly generated questions whose reasoning complexity can be controlled.

The framework first extracts a reasoning graph from each benchmark example, then changes that graph to create new test data. These alterations produce different complexity levels while maintaining linguistic diversity similar to the original benchmark. A language model augmented with code is used to ensure that the generated examples receive correct labels. This couples changes to the reasoning structure with a mechanism for checking the resulting answers.

The authors evaluate 15 language models on reasoning tasks across four domains. Almost all perform worse as complexity increases, with some showing substantial declines. The harder generated examples also reveal more model biases. These observations show how varying difficulty can expose behavior that a single fixed benchmark score may obscure and support adaptive evaluation as a useful complement to existing tests.
neurips-2024-darg-dynamic-evaluation-of-.tldr: DARG modifies benchmark reasoning graphs to create tests of controlled difficulty, revealing performance declines and increased biases as complexity rises.

paragraphs: Poisson regression models count data, but fitting it to a large dataset motivates finding a smaller substitute. This paper studies coresets: weighted subsets that approximate the original regression loss within a multiplicative factor of one plus or minus epsilon. It focuses on identity and square-root link functions.

The authors first establish limits on compression. In general, coresets may require size proportional to the number of data points, and related lower bounds extend to arbitrary data reduction up to logarithmic factors. They then introduce a complexity parameter and a domain-shifting approach. When that parameter is small, sublinear coresets become possible, with only polylogarithmic dependence on the number of observations.

The choice of link function also matters. Dependence on the largest observed count is logarithmic for the square-root link, whereas the identity link requires a larger dependence characterized by a tight bound. The analysis additionally improves a bound on the Lambert W function. For root links of degree three or higher, the authors identify limitations of their analysis, leaving any possible extension dependent on other methods.
neurips-2024-data-subsampling-for-poisso.tldr: Poisson regression generally resists strong data compression, but small weighted subsets have approximation guarantees when a proposed complexity parameter is small.

paragraphs: Exo2Ego-V generates a first-person video from external recordings of someone performing a skilled everyday activity. Its input uses four viewpoints arranged around the scene. The task is challenging because the desired viewpoint differs substantially from the cameras' views, while both the person and the surrounding scene can change over time.

The method combines three components in a diffusion-based video system. A multi-view encoder extracts appearance information at several scales from the external videos. A view-translation prior supplies features spatially aligned with the desired first-person view. Temporal attention layers then help maintain consistency between generated frames. These components address appearance, viewpoint alignment, and continuity across time.

Experiments cover five categories from Ego-Exo4D. The authors report that Exo2Ego-V surpasses state-of-the-art approaches, with an average improvement of 35% in LPIPS. This supports the effectiveness of combining information from multiple external views with explicit guidance for the first-person viewpoint and temporal processing. The reported result concerns this four-view setup and the evaluated activity categories.
neurips-2024-exocentric-to-egocentric-vi.tldr: Exo2Ego-V combines four external video views, viewpoint guidance, and temporal attention to generate first-person activity videos.

paragraphs: A graph representation should help identify which graphs are similar, yet graph neural networks can struggle to preserve those relationships as processing progresses. This paper investigates whether consistency across processing stages helps explain the strengths of graph kernels and can improve neural graph classification.

The authors compare the Weisfeiler-Lehman subtree kernel with the Weisfeiler-Lehman optimal assignment kernel. They find that similarities produced by the latter are asymptotically consistent across iterations: similar graphs remain similar in subsequent iterations. Their analysis connects this property to its superior performance over the subtree kernel. This comparison motivates a conjecture that maintaining similarity relationships across neural-network layers can improve learned graph representations.

To test that idea, the paper introduces a loss that encourages graph similarities to remain consistent across layers of a graph neural network. Experiments show significant classification improvements across several network backbones and multiple datasets, supporting the conjecture empirically. The contribution transfers a property identified in kernel analysis into a training objective for more flexible neural representations.
neurips-2024-exploring-consistency-in-gr.tldr: A loss inspired by consistency in graph kernels improves graph classification by encouraging similarity relationships to persist across neural-network layers.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a classifier on a subset of its original classes can sharply reduce accuracy on the remaining classes. This paper examines what causes that decline by separating the quality of the model's internal features from the scores it uses to choose between classes.

In the authors' empirical study, fine-tuning preserves relationships among classes absent from the new training data and does not degrade the features used to recognize them. Those features often become more discriminative. The accuracy problem instead comes from mismatched logit scales between classes included in fine-tuning and those left out. Logits are the scores whose relative values determine the model's predictions.

This finding points to a simple post-processing calibration that brings the two sets of scores into alignment. The authors report that calibration can recover the pretrained model's capabilities while revealing feature improvements across all classes. Their extensive empirical study supports the robustness of these findings, while the explanations they offer are preliminary. The result changes how the observed accuracy loss should be interpreted in the studied setting.
neurips-2024-fine-tuning-is-fine-if-cali.tldr: The study finds that mismatched class-score scales can explain accuracy losses after fine-tuning, allowing simple calibration to recover performance.

paragraphs: Evaluating causal-effect estimators requires knowing how interventions change outcomes, information usually unavailable in observational datasets. Simulators can provide that reference, but building challenging and realistic simulations is difficult. IncomeSCM addresses this by combining patterns fitted from real data with explicitly designed causal mechanisms.

The paper proposes a repeatable strategy for converting observational data into sequential structural causal models. Its two guiding principles are to fit real-world observations where possible and to create complexity by composing simple, hand-designed mechanisms. The authors implement this strategy in configurable software and apply it to the Adult income dataset, producing a simulator that supports multiple causal-estimation tasks.

Experiments compare established estimators on datasets sampled from these tasks. Methods that perform similarly when modeling observed outcomes can nevertheless differ greatly in the quality of their causal-effect estimates. This makes the benchmark useful for exposing distinctions that ordinary predictive evaluation may miss. The findings support the need for estimators and model-selection criteria designed specifically for causal questions.
neurips-2024-incomescm-from-tabular-data.tldr: IncomeSCM combines real observational data with designed causal mechanisms to benchmark effect estimation, revealing differences that outcome-prediction performance can miss.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph embeddings represent entities and relations compactly so that models can reason about connections and predict missing links. KG-FIT enriches these representations by combining information already present in the graph with broader semantic knowledge supplied by a large language model.

The framework uses language-model guidance to refine entity clusters into a semantically coherent hierarchy. It then incorporates that hierarchy and textual information when fine-tuning graph embeddings. The hierarchy contributes global semantic organization, while the graph supplies local relational information. This makes the external knowledge part of the embedding-learning process rather than relying solely on the graph's existing structure.

On FB15K-237, YAGO3-10, and PrimeKG, the authors report Hits@10 improvements of 14.4%, 13.5%, and 11.9%, respectively, over state-of-the-art pretrained-language-model methods for link prediction. They also report gains of 12.6%, 6.7%, and 17.7% over the corresponding structure-based models on which KG-FIT builds. These results support the usefulness of incorporating language-model knowledge through an organized hierarchy alongside graph structure and text.
neurips-2024-kg-fit-knowledge-graph-fine.tldr: KG-FIT improves knowledge graph link prediction by fine-tuning embeddings with text and an entity hierarchy refined using language-model knowledge.

paragraphs: In multi-agent environments, helping others can encourage cooperation but also leave an agent open to exploitation. LASE is a distributed reinforcement-learning algorithm designed to balance these pressures in games where participants have partly shared and partly competing interests.

Agents give portions of their rewards to other players, adapting those gifts according to learned social relationships. Each relationship estimates how friendly another player's behavior is through counterfactual reasoning. Specifically, the method compares the estimated value of the current joint action with a baseline that averages over that player's possible actions. A perspective-taking module infers the action distribution needed for this comparison, allowing gifting to respond to the estimated contribution of a co-player.

Experiments in games extended across space and time show that LASE promotes group collaboration without compromising fairness and adapts its policies to different kinds of co-players. The findings support the use of relationship-dependent generosity as a way to combine altruistic cooperation with self-protection in the evaluated mixed-motive settings.
neurips-2024-learning-to-balance-altruis.tldr: LASE adapts reward gifts using counterfactual estimates of other agents' friendliness to encourage cooperation while protecting against exploitation.

paragraphs: Influence maximization selects a limited set of people to start a cascade that reaches many others. This paper studies situations where success depends on activating an entire connected group, or motif. For example, an advertisement aimed at friends planning a meal may need to influence all of them to achieve its purpose.

Under the linear threshold model, the authors prove that this motif-oriented problem is NP-hard. They also show that its influence function is neither submodular nor supermodular, so it lacks structural properties that could simplify optimization. To make progress, they construct submodular upper and lower bounds on the function and propose a greedy strategy that maximizes both bounds simultaneously.

The algorithm has a stated approximation ratio of tau times one minus one over e minus epsilon, together with near-linear time complexity. Experiments on diverse datasets support its effectiveness at maximizing activated motifs. The paper's contribution is to align the optimization target with group-level marketing success and provide an algorithm with theoretical guarantees for this harder objective.
neurips-2024-motif-oriented-influence-ma.tldr: The paper develops a greedy algorithm with approximation guarantees for spreading influence to whole social-network motifs rather than counting users individually.

paragraphs: Symmetries and conserved quantities provide useful structure when learning the behavior of physical systems. Noether's theorem connects them: symmetries of a dynamical system correspond to quantities that remain conserved. This paper uses that connection to learn both kinds of structure directly from training data.

The method represents symmetries through learnable conserved quantities and fits them alongside the model's regular training procedure. It uses approximate Bayesian model selection, with an objective derived as a variational lower bound on marginal likelihood. The objective includes an Occam's Razor effect that prevents the learned conservation laws from collapsing to trivial constants, without requiring additional manually tuned regularizers.

The authors present proof-of-principle experiments on n-harmonic oscillators and n-body systems. In these experiments, the method identifies the correct conserved quantities and the U(n) and SE(n) symmetry groups, while improving overall performance and predictive accuracy on test data. These results support learning useful physical structure jointly with dynamics, with the demonstrated scope remaining the studied proof-of-principle systems.
neurips-2024-noether-s-razor-learning-co.tldr: Noether's Razor uses Bayesian model selection to learn conserved quantities and associated symmetries, improving predictions in proof-of-principle physical systems.

paragraphs: A policy trained in one environment may perform poorly when deployed somewhere with different dynamics. Earlier approaches modify training rewards so that behavior in the source environment resembles optimal target trajectories. However, producing the desired trajectories in the source does not guarantee that the same policy will perform optimally in the target.

DARAIL adds imitation learning to address this mismatch. After reward modification supplies a policy for domain adaptation, imitation learning transfers its behavior so that a new policy can generate the same trajectories under target dynamics. The method follows generative adversarial imitation learning from observations and introduces a reward-augmented estimator into the policy-optimization step.

The authors derive an error bound under a mild assumption about the dynamics shift. In benchmark off-dynamics environments, DARAIL outperforms reward modification alone and the other evaluated baselines. These findings support separating the task of obtaining useful trajectory behavior from the task of realizing that behavior in a different environment, with imitation providing the transfer mechanism.
neurips-2024-off-dynamics-reinforcement-.tldr: DARAIL combines reward-based domain adaptation with imitation learning to improve policy transfer between environments with different dynamics.

paragraphs: An unobserved confounding variable can bias causal-effect estimates. Text may contain clues about it, but existing text-based approaches can require labeled examples of the confounder. This paper studies how to use those clues when the important confounder is completely unobserved and such labels are unavailable.

The method takes two separate instances of text recorded before treatment. Two zero-shot models infer a proxy from each instance, and the resulting proxies enter the proximal g-formula for effect estimation. The authors prove that this construction satisfies identification conditions under assumptions about the text instances and the accuracy of the predictions. They also show that some seemingly reasonable alternative constructions fail to satisfy those conditions.

Because some assumptions cannot be tested, the paper adds an odds-ratio falsification heuristic to flag whether to proceed with estimation. Synthetic and semi-synthetic evaluations, including clinical notes from MIMIC-III with open language models, yield low-bias estimates. The results support this text-based route to obtaining proxies where suitable structured measurements are difficult to obtain.
neurips-2024-proximal-causal-inference-w.tldr: Two zero-shot proxies inferred from separate pre-treatment texts enable proximal causal estimation under stated identification assumptions.

paragraphs: Polarimetric imaging must preserve information about both the degree and angle of polarization. Exposure settings create a difficult tradeoff: short exposures produce noisy measurements, while longer exposures can introduce motion blur. Both effects damage polarization information, so improving visual clarity alone does not fully address the imaging problem.

The proposed framework combines two degraded snapshots, one noisy and one blurry. A neural network fuses them through three phases, using modules designed specifically for each phase. The approach aims to exploit their complementary information to produce a clean, clear polarized snapshot while retaining the underlying polarization properties.

The authors report state-of-the-art experimental performance, with improvements in image quality alongside preservation of polarization information. The significance is that restoration and property preservation are treated together within the fusion process. The paired-input design addresses the exposure tradeoff by combining observations with different degradations, making both the appearance of the recovered image and its polarization content part of the intended result.
neurips-2024-quality-improved-and-proper.tldr: A three-phase neural fusion method combines noisy and blurry snapshots to improve image clarity while preserving polarization properties.

paragraphs: Vision neuroscience benefits from models that process images effectively and reflect how neural activity evolves over time. Convolutional networks provide strong spatial processing, while continuous-time recurrent networks offer dynamics closer to biological circuits. This paper combines those capabilities in a hybrid architecture.

The resulting models retain recurrent dynamical characteristics while achieving performance comparable to conventional convolutional networks on benchmarks such as ImageNet. They also show greater noise robustness, which the authors connect to noise-suppressing mechanisms in recurrent dynamical systems. Because dynamical analysis is computationally expensive, the paper develops iterative analysis tools tailored to convolutional structures.

The architecture also serves as the front end of multi-area recurrent networks trained on complex cognitive tasks that previously could not be learned or required oversimplified stimuli. When compared with monkey neural recordings, the models capture time-dependent changes in higher-order visual areas. Together, these results support a framework for studying visual processing that combines image-recognition capability, temporal dynamics, and tools for analyzing the resulting neural-system models.
neurips-2024-recurrent-neural-network-dy.tldr: A hybrid convolutional and continuous-time recurrent architecture combines strong visual performance with noise robustness and biologically relevant temporal dynamics.

paragraphs: Chat models are trained to follow benign instructions while refusing harmful requests, but the internal mechanism behind refusal is less clear. This paper investigates that mechanism across 13 open-source chat models with sizes up to 72 billion parameters.

For each model, the authors identify a single direction in its residual-stream activations that mediates refusal. Removing that direction prevents refusal of harmful instructions, while adding it produces refusal even for harmless ones. These interventions provide evidence that the identified component has a functional role in refusal behavior, beyond simply being associated with examples where refusal occurs.

The authors use this finding to develop an interpretable rank-one weight edit that disables refusal with minimal effects on other capabilities, reporting a simpler and more efficient jailbreak than fine-tuning. They also analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress the propagation of the same refusal-related direction. The findings expose brittleness in the safety fine-tuning of the studied models and demonstrate how understanding internal representations can enable direct control over behavior.
neurips-2024-refusal-in-language-models-.tldr: Across 13 studied chat models, a single internal direction mediates refusal, revealing a vulnerability in their safety fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation requires choosing models and hyperparameters without labeled examples from the target domain. A selection method therefore needs to do more than occasionally identify a strong candidate: it should also avoid selecting the worst-performing option in the available pool.

The paper evaluates eight existing selection approaches across 12 adaptation methods, five benchmarks, and five scenarios. None of those approaches effectively avoids worst-case selection in the study. This makes reliability a distinct concern alongside the usual goal of achieving high selected-model performance, especially when a selection rule must work across different adaptation methods and settings.

The authors identify an overlooked ensemble-based approach, EnsV, and provide theoretical and empirical certification that it avoids worst-case selection. They also show its versatility in challenging settings, including open-partial-set and source-free adaptation. The contribution combines a broad evaluation of current practices with a certified baseline. Its central recommendation is to evaluate protection against disastrous choices alongside peak selection performance when developing future methods.
neurips-2024-towards-reliable-model-sele.tldr: A broad study exposes worst-case failures in domain-adaptation model selection and presents EnsV as a theoretically and empirically certified alternative.

paragraphs: Graph anomalies can involve individual nodes, connections, or entire graphs, and those levels can be related. An unusual transaction, for instance, may connect an abnormal account with a suspicious wider community. UniGAD addresses these relationships by detecting anomalies jointly at node, edge, and graph levels.

Its MRQSampler converts objects from each level into subgraphs, making the different detection problems share a graph-level format. The authors prove that the sampler maximizes accumulated spectral energy, expressed through the Rayleigh quotient, to preserve significant anomaly information. A GraphStitch Network then exchanges information across levels, adjusts how much they share, and reconciles conflicting training objectives.

Experiments show that UniGAD outperforms both methods specialized for individual anomaly-detection tasks and graph-prompt approaches designed for multiple tasks. The authors also report robust zero-shot transfer between tasks. The results support combining a common input format with adaptive information sharing, so that relationships among anomaly levels can contribute to detection while their training requirements are handled jointly.
neurips-2024-unigad-unifying-multi-level.tldr: UniGAD detects node, edge, and graph anomalies jointly by converting them into subgraph tasks and adaptively sharing information across levels.

paragraphs: Molecular inverse folding supports design from three-dimensional structure, complementing methods that predict a molecule's structure. Existing approaches often use separate models for different kinds of molecules. UniIF aims to unify that learning process, reducing the need to develop distinct approaches for each molecular setting.

The unification has two parts. At the data level, a common block-graph representation includes local coordinate frames and initialized geometric features. At the model level, a geometric block-attention network combines geometric interactions, interactive attention, and a module for long-term dependencies. These components are designed to capture three-dimensional interactions within a shared modeling framework.

The authors evaluate UniIF on protein design, RNA design, and material design, reporting that it surpasses state-of-the-art methods on all evaluated tasks. This supports the usefulness of a unified representation and architecture across the tested molecular applications. The contribution is both a common way to organize molecular inputs and a model that can use that organization for several inverse-folding tasks.
neurips-2024-uniif-unified-molecule-inve.tldr: UniIF unifies molecular inverse folding through a shared block-graph representation and geometric attention network, outperforming prior methods on the evaluated design tasks.

paragraphs: Programmatic weak supervision trains models using imperfect labels from sources such as heuristics, crowdsourcing, or pretrained models. It can avoid the need for directly supplied ground truth during training, but that creates an evaluation problem: ordinary accuracy, precision, and recall cannot be calculated directly without knowing the correct labels.

This paper treats evaluation as a partial-identification problem. Instead of seeking a single performance value, it derives bounds on the values a metric can take. Fréchet bounds provide the mathematical basis, and scalable convex optimization computes the resulting performance bounds. The framework covers accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score without requiring labeled evaluation data.

The authors report reliable, accurate, and computationally efficient bounds, including in high-dimensional settings. This makes the method useful for assessing model quality when the usual reference labels are unavailable. Its output expresses performance as a bounded range, giving weak-supervision practitioners a way to evaluate models while retaining the uncertainty inherent in evaluation without ground truth.
neurips-2024-weak-supervision-performanc.tldr: The framework uses partial identification and convex optimization to bound classification metrics without ground-truth labels.

paragraphs: Generating a complete 3D object from one image requires representing surfaces that the image does not show. X-Ray introduces a sequential representation inspired by the ability of x-rays to penetrate an object. It organizes the object's surfaces into multiple layers that can be treated like frames in a video.

Rays cast from the camera center record depth, surface normals, and color at every surface they intersect. This captures both front-facing and deeper surfaces while focusing the representation on surface information. Packaging those layers as a sequence makes the representation suitable for an architecture resembling a video diffusion model. Generation uses two stages: an X-Ray diffusion model followed by an upsampler.

The authors demonstrate generation of both visible and hidden object surfaces from a single input image and report state-of-the-art accuracy in their experiments. The contribution links the choice of 3D representation to the design of the generative model: layered surface sequences provide a compact format that can be processed using ideas from video generation.
neurips-2024-x-ray-a-sequential-3d-repre.tldr: X-Ray represents 3D objects as sequences of surface layers, enabling diffusion-based generation of visible and hidden surfaces from one image.
